context.in_practice: There is only one route here (route 1), and every implementation took it. Every scenario the tool is supposed to handle has its own test. Each test runs the command against a throwaway sample project (a temporary 'theatre') and compares what gets printed against the expected output character for character. Some tests run the command inside the test process and some start it as a separate program. On top of that, one check launches the tool the way a real user would, through the installed `troupe` command, to confirm it starts. For a user, this means the printed messages and exit statuses they see are the ones that were checked, and the tool is known to start from a real install. For a maintainer, it means any change to wording, spacing or exit status fails a test, even when the change was intended. So deliberate changes to output also mean updating the expected text. The tests never touch a real project, because each one builds and discards its own.
context.stakes: Whether the command-line tool people actually type behaves exactly as promised. If it isn't tested the way people really run it, the tool can pass every check and still print wrong text, give the wrong exit status, or not start at all once installed.
context.tradeoff: Route 1: strong guarantees that the output matches and the tool starts from a real install, but every intended change to wording or spacing means updating the expected text, and the tests that start a separate program run more slowly.

plan_why: The question is about how the CLI is tested (the test suite's structure and an `uv run troupe` smoke test). That is about test structure and process, and it changes nothing the CLI does, so no command run against the final code can show a difference between routes. There is also only one route, chosen unanimously, so there is nothing to compare.
routes: Byte-exact CLI tests against temporary theatres (in-process or subprocess), plus a real `uv run troupe` smoke test
